reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A rare, non-inherited disorder of middle-aged and older adults combining diffuse gastrointestinal polyposis with characteristic ectodermal changes
The ectodermal features are alopecia, nail dystrophy or onycholysis, and skin hyperpigmentation
Gastrointestinal symptoms include watery diarrhoea, weight loss, abdominal pain and dysgeusia, often with a protein-losing enteropathy
Numerous hamartomatous-type polyps stud the stomach, small bowel and colon while the oesophagus is typically spared
Malabsorption produces hypoproteinaemia, electrolyte disturbance and deficiencies of vitamins and trace elements
It is thought to be immune-mediated and treatment centres on nutritional support with corticosteroids and other immunosuppression
There is an associated increased risk of gastrointestinal malignancy warranting surveillance
reference.pathophysiology: Cronkhite-Canada syndrome is a rare acquired condition characterised by diffuse gastrointestinal polyposis together with ectodermal abnormalities. The polyps are inflammatory and hamartomatous in type, with oedematous, inflamed lamina propria and cystic gland dilatation, and they diffusely involve the stomach, small intestine and colon. The cause is uncertain but growing evidence points to an autoimmune or chronic inflammatory mechanism, supported by the presence of IgG4-positive plasma cells in some cases and response to immunosuppression. Widespread mucosal disease leads to malabsorption and a protein-losing enteropathy, producing the hypoalbuminaemia, electrolyte loss and nutritional deficiencies that dominate the clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Hyperplastic and inflammatory polyposis from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Upper and lower endoscopy with biopsy to characterise the diffuse polyposis
Serum albumin, immunoglobulins and micronutrient levels
Faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin clearance to confirm protein-losing enteropathy
Assessment of electrolytes and trace elements including zinc and copper
Surveillance imaging and endoscopy for associated malignancy
redFlags: Severe hypoalbuminaemia with oedema and effusions
Gastrointestinal bleeding or an obstructing or suspicious polyp raising concern for malignancy
Severe electrolyte disturbance from high-volume diarrhoea
reference.prognosis: The syndrome can be serious with significant mortality from malnutrition and complications, but many patients improve with nutritional support and immunosuppression; the associated cancer risk means long-term surveillance is required.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for an inherited polyposis syndrome and missing the ectodermal clues
Overlooking and undertreating the protein-losing enteropathy and micronutrient deficiencies
Attributing the diarrhoea to a functional disorder despite systemic features
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Treat the underlying immune-mediated inflammation with corticosteroids as first-line therapy, adding steroid-sparing immunosuppressants such as azathioprine where response is inadequate or relapse occurs

Provide aggressive nutritional support with high-protein feeding and correction of electrolytes, vitamins and trace elements including zinc and copper, escalating to enteral or parenteral nutrition when needed
Manage the protein-losing enteropathy and hypoalbuminaemia, and offer acid suppression and Helicobacter pylori eradication where present, as symptomatic adjuncts
Undertake endoscopic and imaging surveillance for the associated gastrointestinal malignancy risk
Monitor serum albumin, electrolytes and micronutrient levels to guide replacement
Reserve surgery for complications such as bleeding, obstruction or malignancy
Coordinate care through a gastroenterology-led multidisciplinary team with dietetic input
